title: Hearts not yet soft?
hook: has the time not come for believers' hearts to humble themselves (57:16)

segments.voice: Yesterday, ma'akum, and your line was wherever you are. Did you say it at the door of a new place? Day six hundred thirteen.

There's a story told about a man named Fudayl ibn 'Iyad. In his youth, the story goes, he was a highway robber. One night he was climbing a wall to meet someone he shouldn't, and from a house nearby he heard a voice reciting the Qur'an. It was one verse, a question. He stopped on the wall and answered it out loud: yes, Lord, the time has come. He climbed down a different man, and the story remembers him afterward as an ascetic and a teacher. Today, that question.
screen: `A ROBBER ON A WALL AT NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Surah Al-Hadid, verse sixteen. Pickthall: "Is not the time ripe for the hearts of those who believe to submit to Allah's reminder and to the truth which is revealed". In Arabic it opens: alam ya'ni lilladhina amanu an takhsha'a qulubuhum. Notice who's being asked. Not unbelievers. Those who believe. The question is for people who already pray, already know the words. Has the time not come for their hearts to soften? The verb is takhsha'a, from khushu', the humble stillness that's meant to fill prayer. A heart with khushu' is a heart that has stopped resisting. Sahih Muslim preserves a striking line from the companion Ibn Mas'ud. He said that between the time they accepted Islam and the time God reproached them with this verse, there were only four years. Four years in, and already the question came: have you gotten used to it? The verse goes on to warn against hearts that grow hard as time stretches on. Then the very next verse offers the turn. Know, it says, that God brings the earth back to life after its death. A dead field after rain. Commentators read the two verses together: hardness isn't permanent, and a heart can be revived the way the ground is. Read that way, the Fudayl story, whatever its historical details, is the next verse acted out: a hard heart turned over in one night. And the verse's question has no date written on it. It stays open, for whoever hears it.
screen: `ASKED OF THOSE WHO BELIEVE.` · `KHUSHU': A HEART THAT STOPS RESISTING.` · `ONLY FOUR YEARS IN.` · `THE EARTH REVIVED AFTER ITS DEATH.`

segments.voice: The practice: let one hardness go. Sit, and breathe. Notice where you hold tension: jaw, shoulders, hands. Let them soften. Now think of one place your heart has gone hard: a grudge, a habit you've stopped noticing, a person you've stopped listening to. Don't fix it. Just hold it, and ask the verse's question quietly: has the time not come? On each out-breath, let a little of the hardness loosen. The bell holds the time.
Khushu': the humble stillness of a softened heart, which Surah Al-Hadid asks believers whether the time has come to have. Today's word.
Your line: has the time not come? Today, take one small step toward the thing you just held, a message, an apology, a single kind word. Day six hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Muslim preachers and teachers often recite 57:16 as a call to renewed sincerity, and the story of Fudayl ibn 'Iyad's turning is widely told in sermons and books on repentance.

commentators read it as hope: a hard heart can be revived.

fork.setup: you're Fudayl, halfway up a wall at night, and you hear the verse: has the time not come? what do you do?
options: keep climbing; it's just a voice.
answer it: yes, Lord, the time has come.
go home and think about it next year.
fork.reveal: in the story people tell, he answered out loud, climbed down, and turned his life around.

original.note: Arabic: has the time not come for those who believe? ya'ni means it has become time, it is ripe.

trapdoor: what you thought: a warning to people who don't believe.
what it means: a question put to believers, followed by the promise of revival.
what a scholar hears: takhsha'a from kh-sh-', the root of khushu'; Ibn Mas'ud's 'four years' in Sahih Muslim 3027; 57:17 read as the hope that follows.

notes: Pickthall wording of 57:16 quoted from memory; please confirm.
The Fudayl story is framed as 'a story told'; its chain and sources should be checked.
Muslim 3027 cited from memory for Ibn Mas'ud's 'four years'; confirm.
The remainder of 57:16 compares with earlier recipients of scripture whose hearts hardened; the script mentions only hearts growing hard over time, to avoid a foil. A Keeper may wish to adjust.
